title: "02_Peak_Calling_MACS2"
output: html_document
date: "2026-10-08"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(Seurat)
library(Signac)
library(ggplot2)
library(EnsDb.Hsapiens.v86) # For genome annotations
```

## Load Data
First, we load the saved multiome object containing our RNA/ATAC data, WNN clusters, and scType cell annotations.
```{r load_data}
# Update this path if the RDS file was saved in a different location
pbmc <- readRDS("Multiome_WNN_scType_Annotated.rds")

# Verify the object loaded correctly
pbmc
```

## Setup MACS2
Calling peaks with MACS2 requires the `macs2` Python package to be installed on the cluster and available in your PATH. 
Signac will look for MACS2 automatically, but if it is installed in a specific conda environment on your cluster, make sure that environment is activated before starting RStudio!

## Call Peaks per Cell Type
We will call peaks independently for each cell type (using the `sctype_classification` we generated in the previous script). 
This dramatically increases our sensitivity to find rare regulatory elements that are only open in specific sub-populations.

```{r call_peaks}
# Ensure the default assay is ATAC so Signac knows where to find the fragment files
DefaultAssay(pbmc) <- "ATAC"

# Call peaks using MACS2
# group.by tells Signac to group the cells by their annotated cell type
# Note: This step can take a while depending on the number of cells and clusters!
peaks <- CallPeaks(
  object = pbmc,
  group.by = "sctype_classification",
  macs2.path = "/path/to/macs2" # If macs2 is not in your PATH, provide the absolute path here
)

# See how many total peaks were called across all cell types
length(peaks)
```

## Create a New ATAC Assay
Now that we have a new, higher-resolution set of peaks, we need to quantify the ATAC fragments in each cell against this new peak set, and replace our old Cell Ranger `ATAC` assay with this new one.

```{r quantify_peaks}
# Remove peaks that fall on non-standard chromosomes (e.g., scaffolds)
peaks <- keepStandardChromosomes(peaks, pruning.mode = "coarse")
peaks <- subsetByOverlaps(x = peaks, ranges = blacklist_hg38_unified, invert = TRUE)

# Quantify fragments in each cell for the new peak set
# We use the fragments file that is already attached to the current ATAC assay
macs2_counts <- FeatureMatrix(
  fragments = Fragments(pbmc),
  features = peaks,
  cells = colnames(pbmc)
)

# Get the existing gene annotations from the object
annotations <- Annotation(pbmc)

# Create a new Chromatin Assay with the new peak counts
new_atac_assay <- CreateChromatinAssay(
  counts = macs2_counts,
  fragments = frag_obj,
  annotation = annotations
)

# Overwrite the old ATAC assay with the new one
pbmc[["ATAC"]] <- new_atac_assay

# Re-run TF-IDF on the new peak matrix (SVD and UMAP are optional here if you want to re-cluster)
DefaultAssay(pbmc) <- "ATAC"
pbmc <- RunTFIDF(pbmc)
pbmc <- FindTopFeatures(pbmc, min.cutoff = "q0")
pbmc <- RunSVD(pbmc)
```

## Save the Updated Object
We now have an object with high-resolution, cell-type specific peaks!
```{r save}
saveRDS(pbmc, file = "Multiome_MACS2_Peaks.rds")
```
